about: One child-facing fact per BUILT species, for Joe's sign-off alongside the model, the collection and the name. Drafted, then independently fact-checked. Covers the 97 species in SHIPPED_SPECIES on 30 Jul 2026: the frozen base 24, plus garden (14), home-pets (14), woodland (16), africa (13) and farm (16). The species manager shipped farm, four cage birds and two woodland game birds while this file was being written, and those 22 were drafted and checked in a second pass. animal-slow-worm completed Garden later still and was drafted and checked in a third pass. NIGHT TIME's thirteen were added on 2 Aug 2026 in a fourth pass, taking the file to 113; that collection ships thirteen of sixteen and the three missing want shapes the pack does not contain, so there is nothing to write a fact for. FOUR of the thirteen are flagged, which is the highest rate in this file so far and is the method working rather than failing: the checker refuted the tarsier's eye-bigger-than-its-brain as a repeated factoid, the bushbaby's leap distance as true of the wrong bushbaby, the opossum's pouch as absent in most of the family, and the firefly's flash as absent in the day-flying species and in Britain altogether. All four keep their drafted wording and carry a sourced proposedRewrite, because this file's rule is that an unverified fact stays visibly flagged rather than being quietly reworded until it sounds safe. Species in a collection not listed in coveredCollections have no fact yet — see that field.
notCovered: Every other collection in the roster is unbuilt, so there is nothing to sign off. When the manager ships one, its members need adding here or they reach Joe bench factless. The test asserts full coverage WITHIN coveredCollections only, so a newly shipped collection will not break anyone else gate - which also means nothing shouts. Adding the collection id above turns the tripwire back on. WOODLAND and FARM are the two whose members were deleted with the kit builds and are not covered here; Home Pets IS covered and is complete again as of 3 Aug 2026.
method: Each fact was drafted first, then handed to a separate checker told to REFUTE it rather than confirm it, using web search against zoos, museums, universities, wildlife trusts and government agencies. 'flagged' means the checker refuted the wording, found it contested, or could only reach a weak source. A flagged fact has NOT been quietly reworded to sound safe: the drafted wording is preserved in 'fact', and any defensible alternative the checker could source sits in 'proposedRewrite' for Joe to accept or ignore.
guardrails: Brief S19: UK English, bright, never scary. No predation, killing, death or frightening threat framing. Juno is six and learning to read, so one or two short sentences, plain words, one idea.

fields.check: verified | flagged — my checking, not Joe's.
fields.source: URL the checker actually read, supporting the fact as worded.
fields.sourceNote: What that source says, plus any caveat the checker raised.
fields.proposedRewrite: Only on flagged rows. A defensible alternative wording, sourced. Not applied.
fields.verdict: JOE'S. Leave blank until he rules.
fields.replacement: JOE'S. He may rewrite a fact rather than reject it.

facts.fact: Beavers build dams across streams with sticks and mud.
facts.sourceNote: NWF: beavers build dams across streams from branches and sticks packed with mud and gravel.

facts.fact: Bees dance to tell other bees where the flowers are.
facts.sourceNote: AMNH on the waggle dance (von Frisch): it communicates direction and distance to a food source to nestmates.

facts.fact: Rabbits can see nearly all the way around without turning their head.
facts.sourceNote: Eyes set on the sides of the head give close to 360-degree vision. There is a small blind spot right in front of the nose, which is why the fact says 'nearly' and not 'all the way'.

facts.fact: Cats sleep for much of the day, often more than twelve hours.
facts.sourceNote: Adult cats average 12-16 hours of sleep a day.

facts.fact: A caterpillar changes inside a chrysalis and comes out as a butterfly.
facts.sourceNote: AMNH: the caterpillar forms a chrysalis and reorganises inside it before emerging as a butterfly. Grown-up caveat only: it does not dissolve to 'total mush' as pop science often says, but the wording here does not claim that.

facts.fact: A chick uses a tiny egg tooth on its beak to tap its way out of the shell.
facts.sourceNote: Audubon: a temporary keratin egg tooth on the beak tip is used to pip the shell, and drops off after hatching.

facts.fact: Cows bring their food back up to chew it a second time.
facts.sourceNote: Britannica: cows regurgitate cud from the rumen back to the mouth to be chewed again.

facts.fact: Many crabs walk sideways because of the way their legs bend.
facts.sourceNote: Britannica: crab leg joints favour sideways movement. 'Many' rather than 'all' is deliberate — some crabs do move forwards.

facts.fact: Male deer grow new antlers every year and drop the old ones.
facts.sourceNote: US Fish and Wildlife Service: males shed antlers annually and regrow a new set each year.

facts.fact: A dog's sense of smell is far stronger than ours.
facts.sourceNote: University of Alaska Fairbanks. Published multipliers range from 1,000x to 100,000x depending on how it is measured, so the fact deliberately gives no number.

facts.fact: An elephant uses its trunk to drink, to wash, and to pick things up.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo: the trunk draws up water to drink and to spray for washing, and is dexterous enough to pick objects up.

facts.fact: Fish breathe underwater using gills instead of lungs.
facts.sourceNote: AMNH: fish take dissolved oxygen from water through gills. Lungfish and a few others are exceptions, but the general claim is standard.

facts.fact: A fox's bushy tail is called a brush, and it keeps the fox warm.
facts.sourceNote: RSPCA, in one sentence: foxes use their tails, 'also called a brush', for balance and warmth. An earlier Wildlife Trusts source supported only the name, so this was re-sourced.

facts.fact: A giraffe has seven bones in its neck, just like you do.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo: seven cervical vertebrae, the same count as a human, each one very much longer.

facts.fact: Wild boars love rolling in mud to keep cool.
facts.sourceNote: Wallowing in wild boar and other pigs is primarily about temperature — they have very few sweat glands and the mud cools by slow evaporation.

facts.fact: Koalas sleep for most of the day up in the gum trees.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo Global fact sheet: koalas spend roughly 19-20 hours a day resting or sleeping, and are arboreal.

facts.fact: Male lions grow a big furry mane around their head.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo: the mane starts growing around age one and fills in by about five. Caveat: males in some hot regions grow little or no mane, so this is typical rather than universal.

facts.fact: Most monkeys have a tail, but apes do not.
facts.sourceNote: Britannica: almost all monkeys have tails and apes do not. 'Most' covers tailless exceptions such as the Barbary macaque.

facts.fact: Pandas eat bamboo for most of the day.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance: giant pandas spend at least 12 hours a day eating bamboo.

facts.fact: Some parrots can copy sounds they hear, even people talking.
facts.sourceNote: Scientific American: parrots have a syrinx and neural pathways that let them mimic sounds including human speech.

facts.fact: Penguins cannot fly, but they swim beautifully with their flipper wings.
facts.sourceNote: Cornell Lab: no penguin flies; the wings evolved into stiff flippers that drive them through water.

facts.fact: Pigs roll in mud to keep cool, because they cannot sweat much.
facts.sourceNote: University of Missouri Extension: pigs have very few functional sweat glands and rely on wallowing to cool by evaporation.

facts.fact: A polar bear's fur looks white, but its skin underneath is black.
facts.sourceNote: Polar Bears International: the skin under the fur is black and the fur itself is translucent, not white. The reason WHY the skin is black is still a hypothesis, so the fact does not claim one.

facts.fact: Every tiger has its own pattern of stripes, and no two are the same.
facts.sourceNote: WWF, Panthera and the Smithsonian all repeat this, and camera-trap studies really do identify individuals by stripe pattern. But the absolute 'no two are the same' is an extrapolation from the tigers anyone has looked at — nobody has checked, or could check, every tiger. The checker refused to call the absolute wording verified.
facts.proposedRewrite: Every tiger has its own pattern of stripes. Scientists use them to tell tigers apart.

facts.fact: A hedgehog rolls up into a prickly ball when it feels worried.
facts.sourceNote: Wildlife Trusts: hedgehogs roll into a ball of spines when threatened. 'Worried' is the child-facing word for the same behaviour.

facts.fact: Squirrels bury nuts to eat later, and forget where some of them are.
facts.sourceNote: Squirrels do fail to recover a share of their caches each year. Researchers argue about whether that is true forgetting or deliberate abandonment of awkward caches, which does not change the fact as worded.

facts.fact: Mice have long whiskers that help them feel their way in the dark.
facts.sourceNote: Whiskers are touch-sensitive and especially useful to nocturnal animals such as mice navigating lightless burrows.

facts.fact: Moles dig tunnels with big front paws shaped like spades.
facts.sourceNote: Wildlife Trusts uses the phrase 'spade-like paws' for digging tunnels.

facts.fact: Badgers live underground in big tunnel homes called setts.
facts.sourceNote: Sussex Wildlife Trust: badgers live in family groups in a system of underground tunnels and chambers called a sett.

facts.fact: A baby frog is called a tadpole, and it swims like a little fish.
facts.sourceNote: NHM: tadpoles have gills and a tail they use to swim. No source uses the 'like a little fish' simile itself, but gilled-and-tail-propelled supports it as a comparison rather than a claim.

facts.fact: A toad has bumpy dry skin, and a frog has smooth damp skin.
facts.sourceNote: Woodland Trust: British toads have bumpy warty-looking skin that is virtually always dry; frogs have sleek smooth skin that usually looks wet.

facts.fact: A tortoise carries its hard shell everywhere, because the shell is part of its body.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance: the spine and ribs are fused to the carapace, so the shell cannot be left behind. Re-sourced off Wikipedia deliberately.

facts.fact: Newts live in ponds in spring and spend the rest of the year on land.
facts.sourceNote: Canal and River Trust: newts breed in spring in water and are terrestrial for the rest of the year. True of UK newts specifically.

facts.fact: A shrew is tiny and has to eat very often to keep its energy up.
facts.sourceNote: Mammal Society: common shrews have to eat every two to three hours to survive.

facts.fact: Dormice curl up and sleep right through the whole winter.
facts.sourceNote: Refuted on the word 'right through'. PTES itself notes dormice wake periodically during hibernation and even move nests, and the literature describes torpor bouts broken by arousals. They hibernate for months, but not continuously.
facts.proposedRewrite: Dormice curl up in a cosy nest and sleep for months all through the winter.

facts.fact: A vole looks like a mouse but has a rounder face and a shorter tail.
facts.sourceNote: Wildlife Trusts: voles have blunter, rounder faces, smaller ears and eyes, and shorter tails than mice.

facts.fact: A slow-worm looks like a little snake, but it is really a lizard with no legs.
facts.sourceNote: Wildlife Trusts, in as many words: 'The slow worm is neither a worm nor a snake, but is, in fact, a legless lizard', and it has eyelids and a sheddable tail that snakes do not. The independent checker, which never saw this draft, could not refute it and reached three authorities that support it as worded: Wildlife Trusts, Froglife ('a type of legless lizard and are often mistaken for snakes') and Woodland Trust ('While slow worms may look like snakes, they are actually legless lizards.'). It offered blinking as an alternative delight — four authorities back it — but found nothing wrong with this wording, so the wording stands.

facts.fact: A salamander can grow a new leg if it loses one.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian: a lost limb grows back at the right size and orientation. Best documented in the axolotl, which is a salamander.

facts.fact: A corn snake's tummy is checked black and white, like a tiny chessboard.
facts.sourceNote: WRITTEN 2 Aug ALONGSIDE THE MODEL AND NOT YET CHECKED BY ANYONE — flagged for that reason alone, not because the claim is doubted. The black-and-white chequered ventral pattern is the standard description of the species and is one of the two usual explanations for the name (the other being that they were found around stored maize). NO SOURCE WAS FETCHED, so the field is deliberately empty rather than filled with a plausible-looking URL. It wants the same fact-checking pass every other entry here had before it goes to Joe. The fact was chosen to obey the guardrails: a snake's obvious fact is how it catches food, and predation framing is banned, so this one points at a marking a child can see on the model — the pale belly the assembly paints from its own `belly` slot.

facts.fact: Goldfish were once plain grey-green carp. People in China found rare orange ones and bred more.
facts.sourceNote: Wang et al. 2013 (PMC3602300) localises goldfish domestication to Hangzhou and Jiaxing in Zhejiang, China, records that wild Carassius can naturally turn from grey to red, and that those red fish were first collected into Buddhist free-life ponds and only then bred deliberately. Chen et al., PNAS 2020 (PMC7703540) adds the timeline — red scales on 'normally gray or silver crucian carp' first recorded in the Jin dynasty (AD 265-420), selection into ornamental ponds by the Tang, the gold variety reserved for the imperial family by the Song — and the Invasive Species Centre records that feral goldfish revert to olive-green within a few generations, which is the cleanest proof that human choosing is the only reason they stay orange. DRAFTED AND CHECKED BY TWO AGENTS, THE SECOND OF WHICH NEVER SAW THE FIRST'S SOURCES (JT-031's method). The refuting pass could not break the claim but earned one change: the first draft said 'people in China bred the orange ones', which slightly overstates human agency — the mutation arose on its own and was FOUND before it was bred, so 'found rare orange ones and bred more' is the version above. It was then cut from 30 words to 16 to meet this file's own twenty-word cap. Remaining caveats, neither reaching falsehood: the ancestor is specifically the crucian carp, and the earliest records say red and gold rather than orange.

facts.fact: Baby crocodiles chirp inside their eggs when they are ready to hatch. Their mother hears them and digs them out.
facts.sourceNote: Chabert, Vergne et al. 2015 (PMC4616036) states that females guarding their nest react to the calls of near-term embryos by providing assistance during the hatching process, across Nile crocodile, alligator, caiman, Morelet's and Orinoco crocodile. The IUCN Crocodile Specialist Group (iucncsg.org/pages/Reproduction.html, http only, which is why it is not the source field) states the same as a general crocodilian pattern: hatchling embryos 'begin calling from within their eggs', females 'usually excavate the nests' in response, and hatchlings making their own way out is 'the exception rather than the rule'. The causal link is experimental, not anecdotal: Vergne and Mathevon, Current Biology 2008, played pre-hatching calls at Nile crocodile nests and 8 of 10 females dug, against 1 of 10 for noise controls. The Australian Museum's estuarine crocodile page supplies the word 'chirp' and the same behaviour independently. DRAFTED AND CHECKED BY TWO AGENTS, THE SECOND OF WHICH NEVER SAW THE FIRST'S SOURCES (JT-031's method); it could not break the claim. Three caveats it raised, all survivable: the playback experiments are Nile crocodile only, so 'crocodiles' generally rests on the CSG's descriptive statement rather than on multi-species trials; the 2024 follow-up finds that only SUSTAINED calling triggers digging, so 'hears them and digs them out' compresses a threshold; and the Nile crocodile's call is usually transcribed as a grunt rather than a chirp, though 'chirp' is the Australian Museum's own word for it. CHOSEN AGAINST THE GUARDRAIL, NOT DESPITE IT: every obvious crocodile fact is a predation fact, and the mother-carries-her-babies-in-her-mouth one — true, and confirmed on the same page — was rejected because a six-year-old has no mental model for a carrying mouth, only for an eating one.

facts.fact: Wolves howl to find the rest of their family when they are far apart.
facts.sourceNote: International Wolf Center distinguishes two howl types and states the 'social howl' is 'used to locate one another, rally together and possibly just for fun', and that howling is 'the one form of communication used by wolves that is intended for long distance'. That supports the claim as worded. Caveats: (a) reassembly is one of several functions, not the function — the same page gives a 'defensive howl' used 'to keep the pack together and strangers away', and howling also works with scent-marking in territorial spacing; (b) the claim does not say 'only reason', so it is not overstated; (c) 'family' is the correct modern framing — wolf packs are family groups, not dominance hierarchies. I could not read the 2023 Yellowstone triggers-and-consequences study (Canadian Journal of Zoology, cdnsciencepub.com) — 403 — so I did not cite it; secondary reporting of it gives howling accompanying reunions in 20% of 59 events, i.e. real but not dominant. Nothing here frightens, and no predation is implied.

facts.fact: A raccoon's paws are almost like little hands. They can grab nuts, fruit and even bin lids.
facts.sourceNote: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology): 'The forepaws resemble slender human hands and make the raccoon unusually dexterous' and 'Their human-like forepaws are especially sensitive and enable the raccoon to handle and pry open prey and climb with ease. They usually pick up food with their front paws before putting it in their mouth.' The same page lists 'wild grapes, cherries, apples, persimmons, berries, and acorns', plus 'beech nuts, and walnuts', and says raccoons 'have adapted to include trash' in urban areas — so nuts, fruit and rubbish are all covered. 'Almost like little hands' is the right hedge: raccoons have five digits but no opposable thumb, so they are not hands. On 'bin lids', ADW says only 'trash'; the bin-opening behaviour is well attested but my corroboration was news video (CBC, Toronto green bins with a 90-degree twist latch defeated in under 30 seconds), not a scholarly source. UK English is correct ('bin', not 'trash can'). Nothing frightening; 'pry open prey' appears in the source but not in the claim.

facts.fact: A fennec fox has huge ears that help it stay cool in the hot desert.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian's National Zoo says fennec fox ears 'can grow to between 4 to 6 inches (10.2 to 15.2 centimeters) in length', are 'the largest ears relative to their body size of any member of the canid family', and that the fox uses them 'to dispel heat and track down prey underneath the sand'. So 'huge ears that help it stay cool' is supported as worded. Caveats: (a) the ears are not the only cooling mechanism — the same page notes 'Extreme panting helps fennec foxes keep their temperatures regulated ... breathing rates climb from 23 breaths per minute to up to 690'; the claim says 'help', which is correctly partial, not exclusive; (b) heat dissipation is one of two functions, the other being hearing, but the claim does not exclude that. I searched specifically for a contested reading of the Noll-Banholzer (1979) and Maloiy (1982) thermoregulation work and found no source arguing the ears do not shed heat; the paywalled Journal of Zoology paper itself I could not read. 'Prey' does not appear in the claim, so nothing frightening.

facts.fact: A tarsier has huge round eyes. Each eye is bigger than the tarsier's brain.
facts.sourceNote: REFUTED AS WORDED — 'bigger than' is repeated, not measured. The open-access craniofacial growth paper on fetal Tarsius bancanus states that 'Although in each specimen the combined volume of the eyes is less than that of the endocranium, the rate of eye growth against MQ is significantly greater than that for the endocranium', and concludes only that eye size 'may exceed brain size following further postnatal development and supports earlier reports that the tarsier eyes are the same or greater than the size of the brain'. That is a hedged inference ('may exceed', 'same or greater'), not a measurement of an adult eye exceeding an adult brain. Secondary sources contradict each other on the same point — variously 'about the size of their entire brain', 'weighs nearly as much as the animal's brain', and 'weighs more than their brain' — which is the signature of a repeated factoid. Two further problems: (1) the comparison is documented for Tarsius bancanus (Sprankel's eye/brain preparation), and the claim asserts it of 'a tarsier' generically, covering roughly a dozen species; (2) Michigan State University's brain museum page for the Philippine tarsier (Tarsius syrichta) gives 'the diameter of the eyeball being about 16 mm' and offers no eye-versus-brain comparison at all. I could not read Collins (2005), Anatomical Record — 402 paywall — so I am not citing it. The safe wording is parity, which every source agrees on.
facts.proposedRewrite: A tarsier has huge round eyes. Each eye is about as big as its brain.

facts.fact: A bushbaby can leap several metres through the trees in one big jump.
facts.sourceNote: REFUTED AS A GROUP CLAIM — 'a bushbaby' covers roughly twenty galago species and the distance holds for the small ones only. Animal Diversity Web's account of the greater (thick-tailed) bushbaby, Otolemur crassicaudatus — a large, commonly exhibited bushbaby a child would absolutely call a bushbaby — says it makes 'leaps of up to 2 meters' and that 'Locomotion in O. crassicaudatus is generally quadrupedal unless disturbed'. Two metres is not 'several metres', and this species mostly walks rather than leaps. By contrast ADW's lesser bushbaby account (https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Galago_senegalensis/, also read) says 'jumping as far as 3 to 5 meters in a single leap'. The measured biomechanics literature is more conservative still: the highest reliably reported galago jump I found quoted is 2.25 m. So the figure is both species-dependent and softer than the popular numbers. Suggest dropping the distance and the size ambiguity rather than trying to pick a number.
facts.proposedRewrite: A small bushbaby has springy back legs and can leap a long way between trees.

facts.fact: An aye-aye taps on tree branches with its long thin finger and listens carefully.
facts.sourceNote: Duke Lemur Center: 'As they walk along a branch, the animals continuously and rapidly tap it with their middle finger. Cupping their huge ears forward, the aye-aye listens intently to the echoing sounds coming from the tapped tree.' It also confirms the finger's shape — 'their third finger is thinner than the others' and 'slender and highly flexible' — so 'long thin finger' is accurate, and 'listens carefully' matches 'listens intently'. The behaviour is the well-established percussive foraging / tap-scanning, reported at 5-41% of foraging time. Caveats worth knowing but not fatal: (a) the claim says 'branches'; the animals tap branches and trunks, and the Duke wording says 'branch', so this is fine; (b) what follows the tapping is gnawing through bark and hooking out grubs, which the claim wisely omits — keeping it at 'taps and listens' avoids anything a six-year-old would find unpleasant; (c) no absolutes and no group problem — the aye-aye is a single species, Daubentonia madagascariensis.

facts.fact: A baby opossum grows inside its mother's pouch for about two months.
facts.sourceNote: REFUTED AS A GROUP CLAIM — most opossums do not have a pouch. Animal Diversity Web's family account for Didelphidae states: 'In general, the larger members of the family have a pouch; smaller members may have simple lateral folds on their abdomen instead', and specifies 'Larger species, such as members of the genera Didelphis, Chironectes, Philander and Lutreolina, typically have a pouch', while 'smaller species have lateral abdominal folds located near their mammae'. Didelphidae has well over a hundred species and the pouchless ones are the majority — mouse opossums (Marmosa, Marmosops), short-tailed opossums (Monodelphis) and the brown four-eyed opossum (Metachirus) are all described as pouchless. So 'an opossum' generically is wrong. The TIMING, however, is right for the animal actually meant: ADW's Virginia opossum account (https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Didelphis_virginiana/, also read) gives gestation of 'only 12 to 13 days' and says the young 'remain attached to the mammae for approximately 50 to 70 days' — 50-70 days is 'about two months'. The fix is simply to name the species. Note also that the young are attached to a teat inside the pouch rather than loose in it, but 'grows inside its mother's pouch' is a fair simplification for a six-year-old.
facts.proposedRewrite: A baby Virginia opossum grows in its mother's pouch for about two months.

facts.fact: A civet comes out at night, and one of its favourite foods is wild fruit.
facts.sourceNote: Animal Diversity Web on the Asian palm civet: 'They are only active during the night, resting in trees during the day' and 'they are mostly frugivorous, preferring berries and pulpy fruits over anything else'. Both halves of the claim hold, and hold for more than one species — African civets are described as eating mainly fruit supplemented with animal matter, and dietary studies of common and brown palm civets put fruit and seeds anywhere from about 39% to about 96% of intake depending on site and method. Nocturnality is effectively universal across Viverridae. Caveats I would still raise: 'Civet' is a generic name covering roughly 15-20 species, and a few are not fruit-eaters — the otter civet (Cynogale bennettii) takes fish, crabs and molluscs, and several Hemigalinae are largely invertebrate feeders. So the fruit half is true of most civets but not all. I judged that short of a refutation because the claim says 'one of its favourite foods', not 'all civets eat mainly fruit', and because the civet a child would be shown is a palm or African civet. If the game art shows an otter civet, this row should be re-opened. 'Wild fruit' is a good choice of words — it avoids the farmed-coffee-cherry association.

facts.fact: A kinkajou holds onto branches with its long tail while it reaches for fruit.
facts.sourceNote: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance states of the kinkajou's tail: 'The tail is for balance, to hold onto branches while reaching for food, and even to snuggle with while sleeping' — which is the claim almost word for word, including the 'while it reaches for' construction. On the food, the same page says 'Although kinkajous are classified as carnivores (they have canine teeth), most of their diet is fruit and nectar', so 'reaches for fruit' is right. Caveats: (a) the tail is prehensile and long (longer than head and body), so 'long tail' is accurate, though some sources call it only 'slightly prehensile' — the grip is real enough that the animal can hang from it; (b) Potos flavus is a single species, so there is no generic-name problem here; (c) no absolute is asserted — the draft sensibly avoided the 'only carnivore with a prehensile tail' line, which is shaky anyway since the binturong has one too. Nothing frightening.

facts.fact: A nightjar's feathers look just like tree bark, so it is very hard to spot.
facts.sourceNote: Woodland Trust (UK) describes the European nightjar as having 'grey-brown mottled plumage that resembles the bark of a tree', and says eggs are laid directly on the ground 'where their bark-like camouflage helps them resemble a log'. RSPB material likewise describes 'mottled, streaked and barred feathers' creating 'the perfect illusion of bark'. So 'look just like tree bark, so it is very hard to spot' is supported by two UK conservation bodies, in those words. Caveats: (a) 'Nightjar' is a generic name for a family of roughly a hundred species, but cryptic bark-and-dead-leaf plumage is a family-wide trait, so the generalisation is safe here; (b) strictly the camouflage is often described as resembling dead leaves or a log on the ground as much as bark on a trunk — nightjars roost lengthways along branches and on the ground — so 'tree bark' is a slight narrowing, not an error; (c) 'very hard to spot' is a comfortable non-absolute, and the reason for the camouflage (avoiding being eaten) is correctly left unsaid.

facts.fact: A kiwi is the only bird with its nostrils right at the tip of its beak.
facts.sourceNote: I attacked this one hardest and could not break it. Save the Kiwi (the NZ national kiwi recovery organisation) states the kiwi is 'the only bird in the world with external nostrils at the tip of its long beak'. Te Papa, New Zealand's national museum, independently says 'Kiwi are the only birds with nostrils on the tips of their beaks'. I searched specifically for counterexamples — snipe, woodcock, ibis, tubenosed seabirds — and found none: the PLOS ONE bill-tip anatomy paper (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3828210/, read in full) compared kiwi with probing shorebirds and reports 'Kiwi differed from all other species in that the nares were positioned near the bill-tip'; snipes and ibises converge on bill-tip mechanoreceptor organs but not on nostril position, and Procellariiformes have tubular nostrils at the BASE of the bill. Two caveats to record: (1) that same peer-reviewed paper says 'near the bill-tip' and 'near the tip of the bill', slightly softer than the claim's 'right at the tip' — the openings are just behind the very end and are downward-facing, 'shielded dorsally by curtains of keratin'; (2) 'the only bird' is an absolute about every bird that has ever lived, and every source I read is really asserting it of living birds — no source I found addresses extinct taxa, so the claim is unfalsified rather than proven for fossil birds. If the project wants zero exposure on absolutes, 'the only bird alive today' would close that gap, but I am not flagging on it.

facts.fact: A firefly flashes its light in the dark, and another firefly flashes back.
facts.sourceNote: REFUTED AS A GROUP CLAIM — the flash-and-answer exchange is real, but only for the flashing species, and 'a firefly' asserts it of all of them. Mass Audubon confirms the exchange itself: 'Male fireflies seek mates by flying around and flashing. Females rest on vegetation and generally do not fly. When a female sees a male of her own species, she answers by flashing back to him.' But the same page divides the family three ways: 'All fireflies belong to the same beetle family, although three groups have different ways of attracting mates. Some fireflies make quick flashes, while other fireflies give long-lasting glows, and still others use invisible chemical signals.' Ohio State University Extension's 'Flameless Fireflies' page (https://bygl.osu.edu/node/2381, read) covers the third group directly — non-luminescent day-flying fireflies that 'use pheromones wafting from the waxy film on their backs to send come-hither signals to a mate'; Ellychnia and Phosphaenus hemipterus are documented examples. There is also a UK-specific problem: Britain has no flashing firefly at all — its lampyrid is the glow-worm of claim 13, which glows steadily and does not flash. Softening 'A firefly' to 'Some fireflies' fixes both. Secondary point: the responder in the exchange is specifically the female of the same species, not just 'another firefly', but 'other fireflies flash back' is a fair simplification and avoids the Photuris femmes fatales business, which is not six-year-old material.
facts.proposedRewrite: Some fireflies flash their lights in the dark, and other fireflies flash back.

facts.fact: A glow-worm is not a worm. It is a beetle, and the female lights up at night.
facts.sourceNote: The Wildlife Trusts (UK) on Lampyris noctiluca: 'The glow-worm is not actually a worm, but a beetle'; 'Females are famous for emitting a greeny-orange light from their bottoms at night'; 'They climb up plant stems and glow in order to attract males, who have large, photosensitive eyes'. All three parts of the claim — not a worm, is a beetle, the female lights up at night — are confirmed verbatim by a UK conservation body, which is the right register for a UK-English game. Caveats I would still put on the record: (1) 'Glow-worm' is a generic name and the biggest counterexample is outside Britain — the New Zealand glow-worm, Arachnocampa luminosa, is a fungus gnat LARVA, a fly, not a beetle at all; the claim is only safe if the game means the British glow-worm; (2) within Lampyris noctiluca the female is not the sole light source — larvae and eggs also glow, and males glow weakly — but the claim says 'the female lights up', not 'only the female', so it is not falsified; (3) the female is flightless and wingless, which is why she glows from vegetation rather than in flight, so a picture of a flying glowing insect would contradict the text. I could not read the Natural History Museum's glow-worm page (403), so I have not cited it.
